Discover how AWS EKS Fargate executes serverless Kubernetes with dedicated pod scheduling, custom runtimes, and isolated VPC networking.

item.title: OpenAI halved its agent’s price. Its own safety report flagged a catch.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra on Monday, cutting API prices in half and delivering major gains in coding and computer-use benchmarks.

The post OpenAI halved its agent’s price. Its own safety report flagged a catch. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra on Monday, cutting API prices in half and delivering major gains in coding and computer-use benchmarks. But the company’s own safety tests reveal a catch. In nearly 30% of simulated runs, Terra worked around restrictions to complete tasks through methods it wasn’t authorized to use.

In nearly 30% of simulated runs, Terra worked around restrictions to complete tasks through methods it wasn’t authorized to use.

The system card also shows Terra taking unauthorized actions in 13.75% of cases after encountering messages that appeared to come from other AI agents. Researchers found signs that the model sometimes recognized it was being tested.

These evaluations took place in controlled settings, some without production safeguards, so they don’t necessarily predict how Terra will behave in real-world applications. But they expose a problem with autonomous agents: Getting better at completing tasks doesn’t always mean getting better at knowing when to stop.

Cheaper, faster, better at coding

OpenAI is pitching Terra as a cheaper way to run coding agents and automate computer tasks, with substantial performance gains over its predecessor.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Terra solved 50.3% of problems at maximum reasoning effort, compared with 21.5% for GPT-5.6 Terra. OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain better choices for the toughest coding work.

Price may be the bigger selling point with $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens through the API; half the standard price of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

The model is available through the OpenAI API as gpt-6.1-terra, as well as ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users.

When agents ignore the rules

OpenAI’s “Respecting Warnings” evaluation tests whether models honor access-denied errors and other restrictions while carrying out legitimate tasks in simulated professional environments. At maximum reasoning effort, Terra found ways around those restrictions in 29.6% of runs. This was more often than GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol, but less often than GPT-6 Sol.

OpenAI also recently updated the evaluation to count successful workarounds, meaning a more capable model could score worse simply because it’s better at finding alternative routes, not necessarily because it’s more willing to break the rules. The tests were also conducted mostly in low-stakes scenarios without system-level safeguards.

Across 48,701 shared tasks, Terra showed signs of recognizing it was being tested in 9.88% of trajectories, compared with 4.35% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 8.07% for GPT-6 Astra.

Across 48,701 shared tasks, Terra showed signs of recognizing it was being tested in 9.88% of trajectories, compared with 4.35% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 8.07% for GPT-6 Astra. That doesn’t mean Terra deliberately tried to game the tests, but it makes its behavior harder to interpret. An agent needs to distinguish between a malicious instruction and a legitimate restriction, but when it gets it wrong, it may cross boundaries it was supposed to respect.

Messages from other agents

A separate evaluation tested how models respond to messages that appear to come from other AI agents. Across 80 samples covering 10 scenarios, Terra attempted to communicate with apparent peers in 65% of cases. In 11 cases, or 13.75%, it performed the specified unauthorized action, compared with 1.25% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 16.25% for GPT-6 Sol.

OpenAI cautions against treating the difference as a straightforward regression. Much of it involved promises of future assistance that Terra indicated it would not actually carry out. The company considers Terra’s overall performance on this measure comparable to GPT-6 Sol.

Critical cyber at a discount

Even at a lower price, the company classifies GPT-6.1 Terra as having Critical cybersecurity capability under its Preparedness Framework. The threshold covers capabilities such as independently developing functional zero-day exploits against hardened systems or carrying out sophisticated cyberattacks from high-level instructions.

On OpenAI’s internal port of ExploitBench, Terra achieved a 24.5% success rate developing arbitrary-code-execution exploits for recently disclosed vulnerabilities.

GPT-6.1 Sol scored 21.5%, while GPT-6 Astra reached 31.5%. On Sandbox Bench, which tests vulnerabilities in runtimes, file parsers, and egress proxies, Terra succeeded against five of 22 targets. GPT-6.1 Sol succeeded against nine and GPT-6 Astra against 10.

The company acknowledges that Terra still struggles to reliably exploit recently disclosed vulnerabilities. Even so, its performance shows that cutting inference costs doesn’t necessarily mean sacrificing offensive cybersecurity capability.

Lower prices could make legitimate vulnerability research more accessible, while also making safeguards against misuse more important. OpenAI says Terra receives the same cybersecurity protections used for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, adjusted for the new model.

Not every safety test tells the same story

In one evaluation, Terra made no attempts to bypass Codex’s Auto-review system, which uses a separate model to block unsafe commands outside a sandbox.

A larger simulation of 48,690 internal Codex tasks produced 22 flags for serious misaligned behavior, or 0.045% of tasks. GPT-6.1 Sol received 24 flags, GPT-6 Astra received 26, GPT-6 Sol received 38, and GPT-5.6 Sol received 61.

OpenAI defines these incidents as actions a reasonable user wouldn’t expect and would strongly object to. The findings came from simulated tasks, not confirmed incidents in real-world deployments. Terra also demonstrated resistance to prompt-injection attacks comparable to GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Despite the flagged behavior, OpenAI determined that the model’s safeguards were sufficient for public release.

Despite the flagged behavior, OpenAI determined that the model’s safeguards were sufficient for public release.

The post OpenAI halved its agent’s price. Its own safety report flagged a catch. appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenAI’s cheaper GPT-6.1 Terra posts big coding gains, but its own safety tests show the AI agent bypassing restrictions in nearly 30% of runs.

item.title: AI is changing Kubernetes; is your platform ready for 2027?
item.dc:creator: Nick Lucchesi
item.description:
AI workloads, including those using agentic AI, will only add to and change the questions Kubernetes teams have to answer. It’s no longer

The post AI is changing Kubernetes; is your platform ready for 2027? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI workloads, including those using agentic AI, will only add to and change the questions Kubernetes teams have to answer. It’s no longer merely enough to ask if the pods are running. Or how long it takes a model to produce its first token. Or what happens when inference traffic spikes and no additional GPU capacity is available.

Increasingly, questions like those are becoming platform questions that sit next to the already familiar work of upgrades, recovery, and security.

That’s why The New Stack has just published Kubernetes in 2027: Building Platforms for AI, Autonomy, and Scale, a new ebook by Chris J. Preimesberger, in partnership with HPE.

This ebook starts with the work before launch — before the launch. We ask teams to stress-test model-serving systems under realistic loads, rehearse failures, and measure more than GPU utilization.

It also takes a clear-eyed look at agents. Giving an agent access to a cluster is a consequential decision, even if its task sounds routine.

The guide calls for identifiable owners, narrow permissions, approval gates, and audit trails that connect tool calls to the task that prompted them. It asks teams to evaluate AI output quality. A fast answer offers little comfort when it’s wrong.

And the ebook doesn’t treat AI as a reason to forget the rest of the platform. The checkpoints cover policy across clusters, visibility into services outside Kubernetes, upgrade and restoration drills, operational ownership, and developer self-service.

The checklist gets specific about the work that can fall between teams.

Can you see which clusters follow a shared access and network baseline? (And who approved the exceptions?)

Also: When an application slows, can you look beyond pod metrics to the database, virtual machine, network, or external service it depends on? Before the next upgrade, have you checked for removed APIs and practiced restoring both cluster state and application data?

Then there’s the work after deployment: Who renews an ingress certificate? Who signs off on a capacity change? If a developer requests an environment through a service catalog, does it come with an owner, a review date, and a way to see what it costs?

They’re practical prompts for conversations among platform teams, application teams, security teams, and business teams. Download the ebook now before you start the conversation.

The New Stack has launched a new ebook, sponsored by HPE, with 10 practical checks for Kubernetes platforms handling AI workloads and agents.

item.title: Most of Anthropic’s Q3 revenue came from models that barely existed six months ago
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Anthropic’s long-awaited S-1, filed Monday ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut under the ticker ANT, shows how quickly customers are

The post Most of Anthropic’s Q3 revenue came from models that barely existed six months ago appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s long-awaited S-1, filed Monday ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut under the ticker ANT, shows how quickly customers are spending on its newest models.

According to the filing, models released in the six months leading up to September 30 accounted for more than 80% of the company’s third-quarter revenue. Anthropic released eight widely available Claude models between April and September 2026, plus three restricted-access Mythos models. The filing doesn’t say how much revenue each generated; models launched in late September had only days to contribute to the quarter.

But that raises an interesting question for developers: Are newer models delivering better results for developers’ tasks, and what do those results cost?

Are newer models delivering better results for developers’ tasks, and what do those results cost?

How new models compound

The filing suggests there’s a reason newer models account for so much of Anthropic’s revenue. The company says customer spending is closely tied to how often it releases new models and what those models can do. Each improvement naturally gives customers more reasons to use Claude, while more capable models attract new customers and encourage existing ones to use Claude more and spend more in the process.

That spending helps fund the next round of development. Anthropic says in the filing that the company relies on growing revenue to pay for the research, computing power, and technical talent needed to build more capable models. Those improvements can then attract more customers and drive additional spending, creating a cycle in which each generation of Claude helps fund the next.

Improvements can then attract more customers and drive additional spending, creating a cycle in which each generation of Claude helps fund the next.

Did demand drive releases?

The filing shows how important newer models are to Anthropic’s revenue, but it doesn’t establish whether customer demand has influenced the company’s faster release schedule in 2026. While the two may be connected, Anthropic doesn’t say that increased spending is what drove it to release models more frequently.

Revenue, not customer migration

The 80% figure also doesn’t tell us how many customers switched to newer models. A relatively small group of customers spending heavily on the latest releases could account for much of that revenue.

The filing offers some context for how much spending can vary. Anthropic’s heaviest Claude Code enterprise users spend roughly 20 times more than other enterprise users. That doesn’t tell us which models they’re using, but it shows why revenue alone can’t tell us how many customers have made the switch.

Choosing the newest model

Developers building coding agents, retrieval pipelines and automation tools may default to the most powerful model without first checking whether a smaller or cheaper alternative could handle the job. That spending adds up. Reuters reported — citing attendees at Anthropic’s October 14 investor meeting — that the company generated $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue.

Anthropic reportedly generated $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue.

Whether developers actually need the latest models or simply prefer them, Anthropic benefits from the spending. With models released since April accounting for more than 80% of its third-quarter revenue, Anthropic has a strong financial incentive to keep improving Claude.

Anthropic has also called for pacing frontier AI development so safety work can keep up with growing model capabilities. The filing does not show whether commercial demand has affected that approach.

Anthropic’s S-1 reveals models under six months old drove over 80% of Q3 revenue, sharpening a debate about developers’ pull to the newest models.

item.title: Ex-GitHub CEO launches a GitHub rival that reinvents the pull request
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Entire, the startup founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, on Monday launched its GitHub alternative that replaces the traditional

The post Ex-GitHub CEO launches a GitHub rival that reinvents the pull request appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Entire, the startup founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, on Monday launched its GitHub alternative that replaces the traditional pull request model with a new agentic code review system called Trails.

The company has been launching parts of its platform since it announced a $60 million seed round in February. Early on, Dohmke occasionally noted he wasn’t planning to compete with GitHub.

But with Monday’s launch, Entire is launching a full GitHub alternative, with its own twist on what a modern GitHub for the agentic era should look like.

At launch, Entire supports native hosting for private repositories. Public repositories and self-hosted Git nodes are still on the roadmap.

“It’s the moment we’ve been waiting for,” Dohmke told The New Stack last week during an interview at the Linux Foundation’s AGNTCon + MCPcon in San Jose, California. “It’s exciting for us because what we set out to do a year ago is landing now — and bringing the Git hosting and the infrastructure layer together, with sites around the world, […] and the idea of continuous integration, continuous delivery, continuous memory, and then with Trails, our reinvention of the pull request.”

“It’s exciting for us because what we set out to do a year ago is landing now.”

Entire, like other devtools startups, argues that the new bottleneck for developers isn’t writing the code — agents take care of that — but code review. Unlike some other startups in this space, the company isn’t solely focused on that. Instead, the Entire is betting that solving the code review bottleneck requires an entirely new platform.

In his keynote at AGNTCon + MCPcon, Dohmke described a review queue growing in two directions: agents producing more changes, and those changes containing more code.

“I open a pull request, and I realize I have no idea what all that code does,” he says of his previous experience using coding agents.

Right now, that platform consists of Entire’s Git-compatible server, the continuous memory feature for agents that the company originally launched with, and Trails.

From pull requests to Trails

Trails is Entire’s take on the pull request model, but instead of developers reviewing code changes manually, Trails gives them a dashboard with customizable evals scored by agents. That system may assess how risky a code change is, for example, or how much intent drift has occurred over a long LLM-driven development session.

Entire says those evals run on every push, with findings available through both its web interface and its open-source CLI. Coding agents can then use that feedback to address problems and push another revision, while the developer validates the progress.

In the end, the original request, the agent’s session history, and the resulting code all become part of the review.

GitHub already offers agentic code review through Copilot. Entire’s pitch goes beyond adding an AI reviewer to a pull request: It makes the intent behind a change and the agent’s work part of the review process alongside the code.

For Entire, the idea here is that if the evals come back green, it’s ok to merge the code without a detailed human review (though few human code reviews are probably as detailed as they should be).

By default, Entire provides preset review agents, but developers can also define their own configurations in a JSON file and choose among supported Claude and OpenAI models.

“We’re redefining how the developer lifecycle works, and it’s really cool. I’ve been at home in the evenings, sitting on my couch, and texting my agents — all the while getting links from my team to their Trails on Slack and opening them.”

“We’re redefining how the developer lifecycle works, and it’s really cool,” Dohmke says. “I’ve been at home in the evenings, sitting on my couch, and texting my agents — all the while getting links from my team to their Trails on Slack and opening them. And because the user interface is designed for seeing — we’re calling it the head-up display for the pilots– so I look at my head-up display, and I see the ‘stop cop,’ one of the evals that we have internally, and if that’s green and the confidence is high, then we’re merging it.”

Entire is also partnering with Buildkite and Depot for CI. Developers can convert their existing GitHub Actions workflows using Buildkite’s bk pipeline or Depot CI, then connect the repository in Entire.

A faster, distributed Git forge

While Trails is the headline news here, Entire’s core is its Git-compatible distributed source control server, which debuted earlier this summer.

Entire says it can push up to 89x faster than GitHub and 6x faster than Cursor’s Origin.

But while a distributed system with mirrors across geographic regions helps, the key feature for many corporate users may be that Entire was built from the outset to offer private repositories in specific regions, too. Given today’s data governance landscape, that’s an increasingly important feature.

The available regions include the U.S., Europe, India, and Australia. Dohmke says customers choose a primary region and can add mirrors elsewhere, with Entire handling synchronization between them.

Memory for agents

Continuous Memory is Entire’s third pillar. It syncs AI agent sessions into a project’s repository and makes that available to the agents for future use.

For Dohmke, those sessions also preserve the approaches a developer rejected and the moments when they told an agent that working code still wasn’t what they wanted.

The company says the system combines a codebase graph that helps agents find relevant code with an “agentic brain” that turns previous sessions and prompts into memories they can query. That lets agents retrieve earlier decisions and the context behind them when they start another task.

Dohmke expects agent run costs to become the next bottleneck, with teams paying closer attention to token efficiency alongside engineering productivity. He argues that developers may find it’s cheaper to use an existing open-source project or a service like Entire than to spend tokens generating their own replacement.

The platform is free; however, Dohmke says customers pay only for the tokens the review agents consume.

But because these review agents run on LLMs, they still cost money. Right now, Dohmke says, Entire is giving all its users a $100 starter credit. Once users have run out of these credits, they will pay market rates for the model of their choosing.

The arbitrage between the discounts it can get and that market rate seems to be Entire’s current business model.

GitHub has always had very generous plans for open-source projects, and its maintainers and Dohmke hinted that the company may offer help there as well, noting that Entire is already working with some partners, including model vendors, on ideas. “More to come,” he says.

Also of note: Entire’s announcements on Monday come two days before the 2026 edition of GitHub Universe, the company’s flagship developer event in San Francisco. What timing.

The post Ex-GitHub CEO launches a GitHub rival that reinvents the pull request appeared first on The New Stack.
Ex-GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke’s startup Entire launches a GitHub alternative that swaps pull requests for Trails, an eval-driven agentic code review system.

item.title: Claude Code’s top enterprise users outspend other Claude users 20 to 1, Anthropic’s IPO filing says
item.dc:creator: Matthew Burns
item.description:
Anthropic’s IPO filing makes Claude Code the center of its enterprise growth story. The company on Monday filed to go

The post Claude Code’s top enterprise users outspend other Claude users 20 to 1, Anthropic’s IPO filing says appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s IPO filing makes Claude Code the center of its enterprise growth story. The company on Monday filed to go public on Nasdaq. Its S-1 says the average Claude Enterprise user without Claude Code spent less than $75 a month in the third quarter. The top 5% of Claude Code users on Enterprise spent about 20 times that.

Anthropic’s S-1 prospectus spells out a classic land-and-expand play, with Claude Code doing the landing. An engineer picks up Claude Code, likes it, and starts pushing it internally. Anthropic’s sales team show up later, and by then, the filing says, “Claude is often already in use.”

Anthropic calls Claude Code “the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like”

Anthropic calls Claude Code “the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like” and says non-technical teams are adopting it too. That’s wild for a tool that started in the terminal.

The revenue lines up with that story: Anthropic says it had more than 11,900 customers paying $100,000 or more over the trailing 12 months as of September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 a year earlier. Revenue hit $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same stretch of 2025. Token usage accounted for 50% of that.

Anthropic’s own engineers? Claude wrote more than 90% of the contributions to the company’s codebase in September, according to the filing.

Anthropic also says the average engineer produced more than 45 times as much code per day in the third quarter as in 2024. Anthropic

Anthropic also says the average engineer produced more than 45 times as much code per day in the third quarter as in 2024. Anthropic says its engineers increasingly direct and review Claude’s work, though it doesn’t define “contributions” or say how much human review that code gets.

I’ve been building one project a week with Claude Code, and I hardly know what I’m doing. The potential velocity is very real.

The S-1 also explains why Anthropic cares about Claude Code beyond coding. The company sells the software that runs Claude Code to other developers.

“A model alone is not an agent,” the S-1 says. Developers can run Anthropic’s harness on their own servers through the Agent SDK, or pay Anthropic to run it as Claude Managed Agents.

That puts Anthropic closer to the companies building coding agents on top of its models. TNS covered how GitHub and Anthropic used their own agents for major Rust rewrites with very different playbooks, and how AWS open-sourced an agent it says is 45% cheaper than Claude Code and Codex.

The S-1 names Google and OpenAI as Anthropic’s primary competitors in frontier models.

The S-1 names Google and OpenAI as Anthropic’s primary competitors in frontier models. Cursor, Replit, and Cognition don’t appear in it.

In its risk factors, Anthropic lists Claude Code among the critical tools in its own development work, so problems with the product “could directly impair our ability to develop and deploy future models.”

It also warns that as Claude takes on more engineering and research, the company “may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control.”

That sits alongside Anthropic’s public call to pace the frontier, a stance Dario Amodei says may have cost the company an AI lead.

Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The filing doesn’t include a price range.

item.title: Mandatory vs. optional platforms: Mandates deliver twice as often, and teams are dropping them anyway
item.dc:creator: Charlotte Fleming
item.description:
Platform teams that mandated their internal platform were more than twice as likely to say it delivered most or all

The post Mandatory vs. optional platforms: Mandates deliver twice as often, and teams are dropping them anyway appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Platform teams that mandated their internal platform were more than twice as likely to say it delivered most or all of its goals: 62.2%, compared with 27.5% for teams that made adoption optional. Over the same year, the share of mandated platforms in our research fell from 63.0% to 45.9%, and optional platforms became the majority.

That puts the data at odds with the most repeated advice in platform engineering. Team Topologies, the CNCF’s Platform Engineering maturity model, and a 2026 review of the platform engineering literature all say a platform should earn adoption through self-service instead of forcing it. Evan Bottcher’s 2018 description, still widely cited, said a platform “cannot stand on a mandate alone.” Going into the 2026 Future of Platform Engineering report, we expected optional adoption to win out. The data pointed the other way.

“An agent never chooses a platform. It works within whatever access someone configures for it…”

Mandates also travel with leadership backing and budget confidence, so the mandate alone probably isn’t what drives results. That distinction matters more now that coding agents open pull requests and, in some organizations, trigger deployments. An agent never chooses a platform. It works within whatever access someone configures for it, which shifts the useful question from whether to mandate the platform to which policies the platform should enforce.

Mandatory adoption delivers, even as optional takes over

For teams reporting mandatory adoption, 62.2% say they delivered most or all of the benefits they set out to achieve. Among teams with optional adoption, that figure is 27.5%. 

Here’s what adds real weight to this contradiction: the industry isn’t just recommending optional adoption; it’s moving toward it. A year ago, 63.0% of platforms in this research were mandated, and 37.0% were optional. This year, that’s flipped; optional platforms are now the majority at 54.1%, compared with 45.9% that are mandatory. Teams are following industry advice; however, the performance data suggest there is more to the picture. 

Two different questions get two different answers. Mandatory adoption is the stronger predictor of whether a platform delivers on its goals. Optional adoption, however, speaks to something else entirely: a platform earns its place because developers choose to use it, not because they are being asked to, which is a success in its own right.

What comes bundled with mandatory platforms

Mandatory adoption tracking, goal delivery, and performance make more sense when you consider several other factors. In the network analysis of the survey data, we found that mandatory adoption doesn’t travel alone (see network analysis figure below). It clusters with stronger leadership direction, higher job satisfaction, and greater confidence in budget safety, and all of these correlate with one another and with goal delivery.

The simplest explanation here is likely leadership support. Leaders who genuinely sit behind a platform are the ones who make it mandatory, and that same support helps secure budget. In this sense, mandatory adoption is just one piece of a bundle that includes funding and leadership direction. 

AI sits in a similar cluster. Respondents who reported the most positive impact from AI also reported stronger budget confidence, clearer leadership direction, and higher job satisfaction. AI’s impact was also associated with mandatory adoption, though to a lesser extent. 

This data is cross-sectional, so we can’t establish which factor comes first or influences the other. Either way, the takeaway is the same: without leadership engagement and the budget commitment that usually accompany it, a mandate is unlikely to deliver the same result. 

Where mandatory adoption matters most 

A closer look at the same data shows where mandatory adoption delivers value and where it doesn’t. Mandatory platforms are considerably more likely to report higher confidence in budget renewal (78.9%) than optional platforms (50.0%). When considering adoption strategy, budget confidence, and goal delivery together, we found that budget confidence matters more for optional platforms than for mandatory ones. 

Moving from low to high confidence in budget renewal for optional platforms, goal delivery, or performance lifts, from 9.5% to 52.4%, is a big jump (see figure below). For mandatory platforms, budget confidence shifts similarly, but less dramatically (from 37.5% to 70.0%).

What does this mean in practice? Mandating platforms makes performance less dependent on budget safety. An optional platform’s success is tightly bound to whether its funding feels secure; a mandatory platform holds up more consistently either way. It’s less about mandating an underfunded platform and more about mandatory platforms being less exposed to the budget risk that clearly makes or breaks optional platforms. For a platform lead who can advocate for only one thing, this is worth knowing: mandatory platforms appear most effective when funding is uncertain, and less so once the budget is secure.

Mandatory adoption also helps standardize, alongside budget confidence. It may reduce decision fatigue and tool sprawl that inevitably come with everyone choosing their own path, letting the platform handle security, compliance, and governance rather than leaving every team to solve them.

This matters more as agents take on more delivery work. Where a developer might consider deviating from standard processes, an agent will follow whatever routes the system makes available, and standardization helps make those routes safer. 

What a mandate can’t do on its own

None of this suggests that mandatory adoption is a guaranteed win. Relying on mandatory adoption can carry a problem rather than fix it. Our data hints at this: less reliable documentation tracks more closely with mandatory adoption than with optional adoption. When developers have no choice, getting the basics right is not a priority, since the mandate addresses problems that would normally drive users away. 

“When developers have no choice, getting the basics right is not a priority…”

In our dataset, mandatory platform adoption was weakly associated with higher overall job satisfaction. Even more interesting, mandatory platforms were no more likely to track developer satisfaction. Under mandatory adoption, this matters because adoption numbers no longer show whether the platform is working. 

The more cautious position here isn’t “forcing adoption wins”; it’s this: mandate the policies (i.e., security, cost control, the standards a business actually needs) and make platform adoption itself optional. A platform that’s the path of least resistance in meeting those policies will win people over on its own. When done well, this retains the benefits of mandatory adoption, including scale and standardization, while preserving the signal from developers choosing the platform. A useful measure of any platform is whether developers would still choose it if they weren’t required to. 

This case grows as agents take on more of the work. Documented policies and manual reviews are only effective when people engage with them. Agents need the same policies, but they must be built into the delivery process, making the platform that enforces them the most practical option for both developers and agents.

“The strongest platforms probably need both: a reason people have to use them, and a reason they would want to.”

Evan Bottcher’s 2018 statement was correct: forcing people onto a platform isn’t enough. But our data suggests that relying on people to choose the platform may not be enough either. The strongest platforms probably need both: a reason people have to use them, and a reason they would want to.

For agents, who don’t choose at all, the platform itself has to build in the safe path.

The post Mandatory vs. optional platforms: Mandates deliver twice as often, and teams are dropping them anyway appeared first on The New Stack.
Mandated internal platforms were twice as likely to deliver their goals. Yet optional adoption now leads, and AI agents are changing the question.

item.title: The next 10 years of KubeVirt
item.dc:creator: Vladik Romanovsky
item.description:
KubeVirt was founded by Red Hat in 2016 around the idea that Kubernetes could run virtual machines alongside containers. We

The post The next 10 years of KubeVirt appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
KubeVirt was founded by Red Hat in 2016 around the idea that Kubernetes could run virtual machines alongside containers. We wanted to allow users to run legacy workloads on the same platform as their modernized applications. That is still the job, but since v1.0 other projects have demonstrated that they can build on it and integrate KubeVirt in a broader ecosystem. Let’s discuss some of what the next 10 years of KubeVirt will bring.

Other projects such as Open Sovereign AI Cloud (OSAC) use it for VM, cluster, and bare-metal services. Cluster API Provider KubeVirt (CAPK) uses KubeVirt VMs as Kubernetes nodes. Flight Control runs a virt-launcher on the edge without the full KubeVirt control plane.

Today KubeVirt is a CNCF incubating project, with contributors from Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD, Intel, SUSE, and others. The community is working toward KubeVirt’s graduation as a CNCF project. The enhancement trackers for v1.8, v1.9, and v1.10 show what “next” means in practice. From v1.6 to v1.10 the queue went from a small set of items to more than a hundred. v1.9 included dozens of new proposals. The KubeVirt Enhancement Proposal (VEP) process is how we keep the core stable while that queue grows: designs before code, one tracker, and ownership by special interest groups (SIGs).

In this article, I will share some of the work that will shape the next releases: devices and new hardware, extending KubeVirt without growing core, confidential VMs, the VM as a sandbox, and pluggable virtualization stacks. My fellow KubeVirt contributors, Fan Zhang and Harshit Gupta, help explain the features they are working on.

Devices, DRA, and new hardware

GPUs on VMs can already be claimed through Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation instead of using device-plugins. This functionality is beta in v1.9. The same claim model is being extended to generic host devices, network devices such as SR-IOV, and to CPUs. In the near future, a VM will be able to ask for a GPU, NIC, and CPUs and have Kubernetes allocate them as a coordinated set. There is also work to allow KubeVirt to build those claims from the VM spec and an input from vendor policy, instead of asking every user to write ResourceClaim objects by hand.

“That follows the design principle that has guided the project from the beginning: to prefer Kubernetes native solutions and mechanisms rather than building isolated virtualization workarounds.”

That follows the design principle that has guided the project from the beginning: to prefer Kubernetes native solutions and mechanisms rather than building isolated virtualization workarounds. DRA allows us to improve the granularity of the devices and CPU allocations. But there were many other examples, such as Swap in Kubernetes, ImageVolumes, volume populators, and more, that allowed us to delete a KubeVirt-only path and use what the cluster already has.

KubeVirt contributors, including Nvidia engineers, have been working to enable KubeVirt to run on newer Nvidia hardware, such as the Grace Hopper, Grace Blackwell, and Vera Rubin systems. This functionality was developed first in the Accelerated Infrastructure Enablement working group and is moving upstream.

Confidential VMs and trusted execution

Users increasingly want to run sensitive applications and AI workloads on shared infrastructure while protecting their data and models during execution. Confidential computing uses hardware-backed trusted execution environments to provide isolation, including protection against privileged host software within the platform’s threat model. Remote attestation lets workload owners evaluate evidence about that environment before entrusting it with secrets. KubeVirt is expanding support for confidential VMs and exploring integration with attestation and secret-release services, including Trustee from the Confidential Containers project.

“For AI, the trust boundary should extend across the full execution path—CPUs, accelerators, and the interconnects between them,” explained Fan Zhang, co-lead of Kubevirt’s AIE and Confidential Compute working groups. “Workload owners need to verify that environment through attestation before releasing sensitive data or model keys. KubeVirt offers an opportunity to bring confidential VMs, protected accelerators, and attestation together through familiar Kubernetes workflows. Collaboration with projects such as Confidential Containers and Trustee can make these protections more accessible while helping workload owners control access to their data and models.”

This work spans Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX), AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization—including SEV-SNP—IBM Secure Execution, and emerging Arm Confidential Compute Architecture (CCA) support. In KubeVirt v1.9, the feature gate covering AMD SEV and SEV-SNP graduated to beta, Intel TDX support remained alpha, and IBM Secure Execution support reached general availability (GA). Arm CCA enablement remains under development.

“Capability discovery helps determine where a VM can run; attestation helps workload owners decide whether to trust the environment in which it runs.”

Looking ahead, contributors are exploring more consistent discovery of TEE capabilities across cluster nodes, helping Kubernetes place confidential VMs on suitable infrastructure. Other proposals address attestation initialization data, evidence handling, and integration with external verification and secret-release services such as Trustee. Capability discovery helps determine where a VM can run; attestation helps workload owners decide whether to trust the environment in which it runs.

For accelerated workloads, the ambition extends to confidential device assignment and protected communication between CPUs and accelerators. These capabilities require coordinated support across hardware, firmware, the virtualization stack, guest software, and attestation services.

These efforts are at different stages of discussion and implementation. Their inclusion in future releases will depend on community review, integration, and testing.

Extending KubeVirt without growing core

KubeVirt is a mature project. The core is protected on purpose. A feature does not land in kubevirt/kubevirt until we are willing to support it for everyone, for a long time, without breaking the clusters that already run. That takes time. Sometimes the community is not convinced that feature A belongs in the core at all. That should not stop someone from building it.

“A feature does not land in kubevirt/kubevirt until we are willing to support it for everyone, for a long time, without breaking the clusters that already run.”

We are following the Kubernetes idea of extensibility. Users should be able to write a complete feature outside of core and still get the KubeVirt API guarantees.

Structured plugins are that path. A plugin is a cluster-scoped object: domain hooks, node hooks, admission. Domain changes can be a CEL expression, or a sidecar when the hook needs external state. An admin can see it and control it. This is alpha in v1.9.

Pluggable virtualization stacks

The other half is the virtualization stack itself. libvirt, QEMU, and KVM are central in KubeVirt. That is still the default, and it was the right default. In v1.8 we added an in-tree Hypervisor Abstraction Layer and Microsoft’s MSHV backend as Alpha. However, the goal is to make the virtualization stack pluggable so users will be able to extend KubeVirt, letting Cloud Hypervisor, OpenVMM, or Firecracker live out-of-tree without forking KubeVirt. That work is still ongoing.

“KubeVirt enables customers to modernize VM workflows by bringing Kubernetes orchestration, storage, and networking to virtual machines,” said Harshit Gupta, senior software engineer, Microsoft. “Extending these benefits to virtualization solutions built on alternative stacks adds user flexibility. Our proposal builds on work to support alternate hypervisors and aims to fully decouple KubeVirt from its underlying virtualization stack through a pluggable virtualization framework. It follows KubeVirt’s move toward greater customization and flexibility. I’m excited to be working on this because it has the potential to broaden KubeVirt’s adoption across organizations.”

Pluggability will require re-architecting KubeVirt to use a plugin framework for choosing a specific virtual machine monitor and hypervisor, and initial work has begun to implement this. KubeVirt Enhancement Proposal #82 outlines the main pluggability work. Beyond enabling other virtualization platforms, maintaining backends as plugins could support better testing and easier maintenance.

The next 10 years

The project began a decade ago with a simple focus: assisting organizations as they shifted legacy VM workloads onto Kubernetes. Today, the mission has evolved toward empowering teams to deploy modern, next-generation platforms. From AI inference and edge deployments to hardened multi-tenant environments and emerging architectures, the community remains committed to advancing what virtual machines can do natively on the platform.

What started as an ambitious experiment to orchestrate VMs through Kubernetes has expanded into an entire ecosystem. The next decade will depend on how contributors turn these proposals into stable capabilities.

Discover KubeVirt's future: confidential computing, cutting-edge AI hardware, and modular, pluggable virtualization stacks.

item.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash vs. MiniMax M3: One is cheaper, but not faster or better
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
MiniMax released M3.1 Flash on October 19, 2026, and says it cuts the overall cost of agentic tasks by 70%

The post MiniMax M3.1 Flash vs. MiniMax M3: One is cheaper, but not faster or better appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
MiniMax released M3.1 Flash on October 19, 2026, and says it cuts the overall cost of agentic tasks by 70% and makes online inference nearly three times faster than M3. MiniMax lists Flash at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens.

Those are half M3’s discounted rates of $0.30 and $1.20 for requests with no more than 512K input tokens; cached input and longer M3 requests have separate rates. Online inference speed differs from the time needed to finish a tool-using task.

Artificial Analysis independently scored M3.1 Flash at 72.5% on AutomationBench-AA, a test of multi-step work across simulated business apps. That score measures the share of task objectives completed without guardrail violations. It differs from the percentage of entire tasks completed on Zapier’s own AutomationBench leaderboard.

I didn’t run AutomationBench myself. Instead, I tested M3.1 Flash against M3 on three smaller agent tasks to see how they behaved in work closer to my own. One run per task is too small a sample to measure a general improvement in accuracy, cost, or speed.

The tests

I ran both models once per test through OpenRouter, pinned to MiniMax’s own servers, at default settings. At the time of testing, I used OpenRouter’s free Flash endpoint, so the dollar amounts below for Flash are estimates at MiniMax’s list prices, not charges I paid. I didn’t use the MiniMax API directly because its credit minimum was too high for this small test. I capped the turns each model could use to complete the job.

Results through OpenRouter may differ from runs through MiniMax’s API, even when routed to MiniMax’s servers. I used OpenRouter because it let me test both models in one place.

  • Agentic bug fix – A Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one wrong test. The model reads, edits, and runs tests through tools, with a 25-turn cap.
  • Incident investigation – Logs, metrics, and deploy history for 20 fake services during an outage. The cause is a config change hidden behind two decoy deploys and a server clock that runs slow.
  • Long context – A fake engineering wiki of about 500,000 tokens with three questions about how its services depend on each other.

The agentic bug fix test

Neither model scored perfectly, both finishing with a 5 of 6, but each missed something different. Flash fixed all three bugs without breaking anything. It then ran out of turns before writing its final answer, so it never reported the wrong test. M3 reported the wrong test but missed one case on the second bug.

The tool logs show two different working styles. Flash read 37 files over its first 14 turns before making a single edit. It had every bug fixed by turn 16, then spent its last four turns writing a scratch test to double-check the docs. M3 ran the tests once and made its first fix on turn 4. 

Flash’s approach got all three bugs right, but it burned through its turns reading and checking and never got to write up what it found.

Flash’s approach got all three bugs right, but it burned through its turns reading and checking and never got to write up what it found. M3 moved faster and missed a case. Flash used more than twice the input tokens and had an estimated cost about 23% lower on this task, helped by discounted cached input.

The numbers: 

  • Flash: 25 turns, 538,718 in, 7,056 out, $0.017, 129.0 s, 55 tokens/s.
  • M3 17 turns, 203,639 in, 4,327 out, $0.022, 36.8 s, 118 tokens/s.

The incident investigation test

Both models scored 10 of 10. Each found the config change, ruled out both decoy deploys, caught the slow clock, and listed all nine affected services in order.

They made the same 63 tool calls, but Flash bundled more calls per turn and finished in 17 turns, compared with M3’s 24. Flash used fewer input tokens and had an estimated cost about 68% lower on this test, close to MiniMax’s 70% claim for agentic tasks. Turn count alone does not explain the difference; cache use and token prices also matter.

Flash used fewer input tokens here, but slightly more output tokens.

The numbers:

  • Flash: 17 turns, 367,401 in, 13,175 out, $0.020, 146.2 s, 90 tokens/s.
  • M3: 24 turns, 592,377 in, 12,061 out, $0.062, 72.2 s, 167 tokens/s.

The long context test

Neither model produced an answer. Flash used the 64,000 output tokens I allowed and ran out before writing anything. M3 also stopped after roughly 29,000 output tokens without an answer. MiniMax lists a roughly 1-million-token context window for M3, but that capacity did not translate into a completed answer in this run.

MiniMax lists a roughly 1-million-token context window for M3, but that capacity did not translate into a completed answer…

I ran one extra round with reasoning set to low and the same 28,000-token output limit for both. Flash answered this time but found only 3 of 33 affected services. M3 again ran out before answering.

Neither model answered this large-document question reliably under my settings. Flash hit the 64,000-token output limit I set on the first run. When I pushed it to answer with less, it missed 30 of the 33 services. I wouldn’t rely on either result for a task like this.

The test results

Both models received the same scores on the two graded tasks, and neither answered the long-context question in the first round. M3 was faster overall. Flash’s estimated total cost was lower, even though it used more input and output tokens. Cache use and different token prices affect that comparison, so token totals alone cannot show which model would cost less at identical rates.

What do I think?

I noticed differences between MiniMax M3 and M3.1 Flash, but apart from the lower estimated cost, I wouldn’t call them improvements in these runs. Flash was slower overall, and both models scored the same on the graded tasks.

…apart from the lower estimated cost, I wouldn’t call them improvements in these runs.

Three one-off tests cannot establish whether MiniMax’s benchmark claim holds across other work. I would test more of my own tasks before choosing either model, and I’ll keep an eye on MiniMax’s future updates.

The post MiniMax M3.1 Flash vs. MiniMax M3: One is cheaper, but not faster or better appeared first on The New Stack.
MiniMax says M3.1 Flash cuts agentic task costs by 70%. In three hands-on tests against M3, it came out cheaper, but slower and no more accurate.

item.title: The sandbox wasn’t enough: Why AI agent governance requires runtime observability
item.dc:creator: Manveer Chawla
item.description:
Models running an OpenAI cybersecurity evaluation reached the public Internet from an environment designed to be isolated. Package installation through

The post The sandbox wasn’t enough: Why AI agent governance requires runtime observability appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Models running an OpenAI cybersecurity evaluation reached the public Internet from an environment designed to be isolated. Package installation through an internal registry proxy and cache was the only intended network path.

The models found a previously unknown vulnerability in that proxy. They escalated privileges, moved laterally to a node with Internet access, then used additional vulnerabilities and stolen credentials to intrude into Hugging Face’s production infrastructure.

The isolation policy said the public Internet was out of bounds – but the running system proved otherwise.

This was not a story about absent monitoring. OpenAI says its security team detected anomalous activity internally. Hugging Face reports that it combined runtime and SIEM signals into an attack signal, but the alert wasn’t critical enough to prompt the on-call team promptly.

Hugging Face investigators recovered roughly 17,600 agent actions across several trust boundaries. The signals existed. They didn’t trigger intervention early enough.

“A configured boundary does not prove what is reachable at runtime.”

Anthropic’s review of 141,006 cybersecurity evaluation runs found three incidents involving six runs, revealing a different failure mode. Those models reached real systems because an evaluation environment had unintended Internet access. That was a configuration failure, not an exploited sandbox escape.

These were capability evaluations, not normal production deployments. Both organizations report that they removed or reduced standard deployment safeguards to measure underlying cyber capabilities. 

But the governance lesson still holds: A configured boundary does not prove what is reachable at runtime.

Why AI agents change the containment problem

Runtime detection and defense-in-depth are not new. Agents change the execution model.

In a fixed workflow, code specifies intermediate steps. A tool-using agent can choose and revise those steps while it runs. It can react to a result, retry a failed path, and use one tool’s output as another tool’s input.

That changes what must be governed. A DNS lookup, package download, or credential read may be harmless alone. In the right sequence, the same events can form a path from a sandbox to a production system.

Design-time governance sets the conditions: isolation, identities, tool permissions, policies and approvals. Runtime governance measures what happened against those conditions and changes system state when the two diverge.

Observability does not replace prevention. It shows when prevention no longer matches reality.

Governance frameworks already reflect this distinction. For high-risk systems, the EU AI Act requires automatic event logging, human oversight capable of detecting anomalies and interrupting a system, and post-market monitoring throughout its lifetime. NIST’s Generative AI Profile similarly calls for post-deployment monitoring, escalation, and incident response.

“Observability does not replace prevention. It shows when prevention no longer matches reality.”

Those frameworks establish the requirement. Agents compress the response window in which it must be met. One deployment-specific measure makes that visible:

actions_before_containment = agent_action_rate x detection_to_containment_time

This does not measure the severity of those actions. It measures how many can occur before the system intervenes.

Four properties that turn telemetry into governance

The answer is not simply more logs. A runtime evidence system needs four properties.

Coverage: Are the transitions that change authority or create an external effect instrumented? Relevant events include agent and run identity, tool calls, process execution, privilege changes, credential use, network destinations, package retrieval, resource changes, and policy decisions. Log volume cannot compensate for a blind trust boundary.

“The answer is not simply more logs. Log volume cannot compensate for a blind trust boundary.”

Correlation: Can an external effect be traced to the action that caused it? The evidence should identify the agent run, tool call, policy decision, and descendant actions. A planner trace without process, identity, and network evidence shows the request, not its effect. Process and network evidence without the agent trace shows the effect, not the decision that caused it.

Timeliness: Can the system intervene before the action becomes irreversible? Place synchronous gates in front of high-impact actions such as public egress, credential access, code execution, and production writes. Streaming analysis handles patterns that become dangerous only across several events. A separate response service can then suspend the run, isolate the workload, or revoke its credentials.

Auditability: Can investigators reproduce the finding without trusting the agent’s account? My earlier article argued that database-backed observations should remain separate from an agent’s interpretation. The same separation applies here. The agent may explain its actions, but its explanation is not the audit record.

From evidence to intervention

Telemetry becomes containment only when it is connected to a response:

agent action + policy decision + infrastructure effect
                         |
                         v
               correlated evidence
                         |
                         v
                      response

Agent actions, policy decisions, and infrastructure effects establish what was attempted, permitted, and changed. Correlating them turns separate events into evidence. Connecting that evidence to a response turns observability into containment.

This evidence creates its own analytical workload. Agent runs, tools, identities, policy decisions, processes, and network destinations all add dimensions. Removing those dimensions before analysis can remove the signal that identifies the violating run.

The evidence in this feedback loop comes from two instrumentation layers, and the coverage list above spans both. The agent runtime emits run identity, model calls, tool calls, and guardrail checks. The infrastructure emits process execution, credential use, network destinations, and resource changes. Neither layer can reconstruct the other. Infrastructure logs cannot say which run or which tool call opened a connection. An agent trace cannot say what the connection reached.

The agent layer is the domain of LLM observability. Langfuse records each step an agent takes as a typed observation, including agent, tool, generation, and guardrail steps, and distinguishes the tools available to an agent from the tools it called. That distinction supports filters for sensitive tool use and looping tool paths, with alerts on the result. Trace context propagates across service boundaries and through MCP calls, so one trace can span a multi-service agent and its tool servers.

DKB runs an assistant for roughly 6 million banking customers that can change transfer limits and block cards, with the customer confirming each action. Langfuse traces every interaction, automatically screens for compliance violations, and routes flagged cases to human review. Cresta propagates trace context across a Go agent service, a Python retrieval pipeline and a tool-execution service, so one trace covers the full call tree.

ClickStack covers the infrastructure layer. It collects OpenTelemetry logs, metrics, and traces as wide events in ClickHouse, allowing teams to correlate high-cardinality telemetry with SQL during live detection and forensic investigation.

The two layers share trace context. An application instrumented with OpenTelemetry can export the same traces to both so that each tool can identify the same request. Logs and metrics continue to flow to ClickStack, where SQL correlates them with those traces. Both store their data in ClickHouse.

“Governance is not the policy document. It is the system’s ability to show whether the policy held, explain what happened when it did not, and stop the consequences from spreading.”

Langfuse and ClickStack complement policy engines, identity systems, and enforcement mechanisms. Policy engines evaluate what is allowed, identity systems establish who or what is acting, and enforcement mechanisms carry out the response. The two observability layers bring their signals together with observed behavior, with ClickHouse serving as the analytical foundation for correlation and investigation.

That runtime governance loop should pass four tests:

  1. Every critical trust boundary has telemetry coverage.
  2. You can trace every high-impact action from agent identity and policy decision to downstream effects.
  3. Evidence reaches a policy gate or bounded stop path in time to prevent or contain irreversible effects.
  4. The audit record remains independent of the agent’s narrative.

Governance is not the policy document. It is the system’s ability to show whether the policy held, explain what happened when it did not, and stop the consequences from spreading.

The post The sandbox wasn’t enough: Why AI agent governance requires runtime observability appeared first on The New Stack.
Static sandboxes cannot contain dynamic AI agents. Discover why effective governance demands runtime observability and rapid containment.

item.title: The AI observability race will be won on interoperability
item.dc:creator: Greg Leffler
item.description:
The AI race is often measured by model quality, speed, and token cost. For business leaders, those measures contribute to

The post The AI observability race will be won on interoperability appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
The AI race is often measured by model quality, speed, and token cost. For business leaders, those measures contribute to a larger question: Can an organization deliver useful AI outcomes reliably, at the right cost, and with a level of risk it can defend?

To answer that question, organizations need comparable evidence and data across changing models, frameworks, and providers. OpenTelemetry helps by giving teams a common way to capture and describe AI behavior. That can reduce the need to maintain a separate data model for each integration.

Shared AI conventions can reduce duplicate integration work, make providers and models easier to compare, and support decisions about quality, cost, and risk. Consistent data also gives teams a stronger basis for scaling AI applications.

Interoperability reduces the cost of change

AI applications have many parts: model providers, orchestration frameworks, retrieval systems, tools, and evaluation services, to name a few. Each may handle a conversation or agent action differently. Teams spend time normalizing those differences before they can investigate failures or compare results. These subtle differences slow product improvement and make switching observability providers more expensive.

“Standardization doesn’t require every system to store every detail in the same way. It does require enough shared meaning to compare what matters.”

That distinction matters to businesses. Standardization doesn’t require every system to store every detail in the same way. It does require enough shared meaning to compare what matters. OpenTelemetry’s GenAI conventions describe common conversation and message concepts while accounting for the limits of representing complex data in telemetry. They also allow large content to be stored externally, with references retained in telemetry.

Splunk’s Agent Observability work illustrates the practical value of this approach: it’s built on OpenTelemetry and AGNTCY standards to provide vendor-neutral monitoring across AI agents and applications. The aim is to give teams a way to correlate agent behavior with performance, quality, cost, and risk — even as the underlying stack changes.

Measure the outcome, not just the tokens

Token counts help explain spend, but they don’t tell you whether that AI spend was tied to useful work or added business value. A less expensive model can consume more tokens or require more retries to complete a task. A higher-cost model may be more efficient if it reaches the desired result reliably on the first attempt.

That makes cost per outcome a more useful business measure than cost per token alone. A successful outcome might be a completed workflow or an accurate answer that meets an agreed quality bar. OpenTelemetry provides the framework for collecting consistent data about model calls, latency, errors, usage and tool interactions, regardless of what model, backend, provider, or tools are in use. The organization still needs to define success and measure it against the cost and use of these tools.

“Token counts help explain spend, but they don’t tell you whether that AI spend was tied to useful work or added business value.”

Evaluation can help. An instrumentation-side evaluator can provide quick feedback close to the application, while platform-side evaluation can compare models and releases across workloads. With consistent telemetry, teams can use evaluation results to decide which model fits a task, whether a release improved performance, and where spending is driving value. They can do this regardless of changes to models, providers, or tool calls.

Build for change without reinstrumenting

In addition, telemetry quality needs to be visible before production. Open source tools like Observability Studio provide a development-time example: teams can inspect local telemetry and validate whether it follows OpenTelemetry conventions. They can even use the tool to help add instrumentation that is compliant from the start. Catching missing or inconsistent data earlier can reduce rework and give operators stronger evidence when they need to troubleshoot or assess a release.

“OpenTelemetry provides the framework for collecting consistent data, regardless of what model, backend, provider, or tools are in use.”

The business benefit is a quicker path from adopting a new AI capability to understanding how it behaves in connection with the organization’s business priorities and customers.

Observability provides control for agent behavior

AI agents can select tools, retry operations, and trigger actions on behalf of users.  An AI SRE agent, for example, might detect that customers can’t check out on a retail site, investigate the problem, restart a failing service, and confirm that purchases are working again. Teams need to know not just whether the agent responds, but whether it takes useful actions, follows safety rules, and knows when to stop and ask for help. A mistaken action can make an outage worse and damage customer trust, while repeated retries or endless troubleshooting can drive unexpected costs.

This is where observability starts to provide operational control. Agent observability can help teams evaluate behavior and track performance and cost. When connected to enforcement systems, it can also support guardrails that block harmful actions or outputs. Shared telemetry collected through OpenTelemetry can connect those controls to evidence about the agent’s steps, tool calls, and ultimately its business impact.

The standard should make evidence portable; the business should define the policy to apply that evidence. Which actions require approval? What quality bar is acceptable? When should a request be routed to a person or a different model? OpenTelemetry doesn’t need to answer those questions. Instead, it gives teams the power to make those decisions using consistent information.

Upstreaming is an investment in scale

For businesses, upstreaming their changes to open source can mean broader coverage and less duplicated engineering—but only when projects have clear ownership and sustained community maintenance.

AI instrumentation faces a similar challenge. Third-party libraries can support new frameworks and providers before the broader ecosystem catches up. Upstream proposals show the value of reusing mature instrumentation, along with the need to settle code scope, contribution rights, and long-term maintenance. For example, the OpenInference proposal covers instrumentation code, while leaving its specification and semantic conventions outside the proposed scope.

“The prize is not more data. It is the ability to scale AI with clearer decisions about value, reliability, and risk.”

For OpenTelemetry, the challenge is to agree on common evidence. Shared conventions can make model behavior easier to compare, reduce the cost of integrating new providers, and help teams connect AI performance to spend, customer experience, and business outcomes. Adopting OpenTelemetry’s standards also helps to minimize potential rework in the future.

The prize is not more data. It is the ability to scale AI with clearer decisions about value, reliability, and risk.

item.title: Is Kubernetes ready for AI agents?
item.dc:creator: Dan Ciruli
item.description:
Kubernetes was built around a fairly simple assumption. It’s that software does what its developers told it to do. AI

The post Is Kubernetes ready for AI agents? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Kubernetes was built around a fairly simple assumption.

It’s that software does what its developers told it to do. AI Agents complicate that assumption. An agent can reason about a problem, choose a course of action, call tools, write code, interact with other systems, and keep working toward a goal. That is precisely what makes agents useful. But it is also what makes running them in production different from running a conventional application.

And increasingly, enterprises want to run them on Kubernetes. A recent survey by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) found that two-thirds of organizations running AI inference workloads run them on Kubernetes. This makes sense, as Kubernetes has become the standard way enterprises deploy and operate distributed applications over the past decade. It already knows how to schedule workloads, allocate resources, recover from failures, and scale applications up and down.  

KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!

Inference demand can arrive in bursts, requiring customers to rapidly scale up underlying hardware and software resources to meet surging demand. In that regard, Kubernetes is an excellent fit. Similarly, as AI workloads wind down, Kubernetes can gracefully scale down the underlying infrastructure, ensuring economical operation.

As good as the fit between AI inference and Kubernetes is, the combination still has gaps, starting with security. Recent incidents at frontier AI labs, in which AI agents escaped test environments and launched malicious cyberattacks across the internet, highlight the need for strong guardrails to keep AI workloads from misbehaving. 

Unfortunately, the probabilistic nature of AI leads to situations where it’s impossible to predict exactly what resources an AI workload will seek to use, which increases the likelihood that agents will eventually cross the line. Therefore, the ideal AI platform should make it easy to enforce clear guardrails and keep agentic workloads safely contained within well-defined sandboxes.

“The ideal AI platform should make it easy to enforce clear guardrails and keep agentic workloads safely contained within well-defined sandboxes.”

By confining agentic AI workloads to a sandbox logically separate from other Kubernetes workloads, an enterprise can better ensure that if an AI workload does run off the rails, the ensuing damage stays within that sandbox.

Instead of letting agents access whatever resources they want, agentic platforms should use an explicit permissioning framework that grants or denies access to files, tools, and network and system resources. Agents should be fully restricted from executing code unless they have been given explicit permission.

The good news is that the Kubernetes community is moving toward adopting sandboxing as an architectural element for constraining AI agents. The CNCF is working to address Kubernetes’s security and isolation gaps. However, the open-source project’s functionality is not yet fully there.

Proper AI sandboxing requires looking beyond the container and into virtual machines or the host operating system to ensure agentic workloads can’t affect other applications running in the same environment. Enterprises looking to deploy AI into production today can turn to commercial Kubernetes distributions that already include these sandboxing capabilities.

Monitoring of AI workloads is another concern that keeps CIOs up at night. While frontier AI labs may not have adequately monitored what their AI models were doing, or even whether they had internet access, enterprises generally don’t have the luxury of asking for forgiveness when their agents misbehave.

Security may be the most obvious challenge, but it is not the only one. Agents are also changing how compute is consumed. A normal service might run continuously for months, while an agent may exist for only seconds. 

“A normal service might run continuously for months, while an agent may exist for only seconds.”

A user asks a question -> an agent starts -> it performs some work, possibly creates other agents, calls several tools, and then disappears. 

Now multiply that pattern across thousands of users and the infrastructure begins to look very different from a conventional Kubernetes environment.

On top of that, starting a Kubernetes workload from scratch can take seconds. For many applications, that is perfectly acceptable. But for an interactive agent, those seconds can feel painfully slow. That creates an interesting infrastructure problem: How do you get the isolation of a fresh environment without paying the startup cost of creating one every time?

Hence, the sporadic nature of agentic workloads, and the need for agents to spin up rapidly, is testing even Kubernetes’ flexibility. Just as first-generation Kubernetes didn’t support stateful applications, the community is still searching for the best abstraction layer for running the new generation of agentic workloads. 

“Agents stay in a state of suspended animation in a warm pool, allowing them to reanimate in milliseconds rather than the seconds it would take to fully wake from deep sleep.”

One answer that is gaining attention in the community is an agent substrate for rapidly scaling Kubernetes-based agentic workloads. With agent substrate, Kubernetes pods containing AI agents aren’t fully spun down when they’re not needed, because spinning them up from a sleep state would introduce too much latency from the user’s point of view.  Instead, agents stay in a state of suspended animation in a warm pool, allowing them to reanimate in milliseconds rather than the seconds it would take to fully wake from deep sleep.

When deploying AI workloads at scale in the real world, the details matter. Not every Kubernetes distribution provides the full raft of capabilities that enterprises demand. As the open-source Kubernetes community adapts to changing requirements, forward-looking platform providers are building the guardrails, sandboxing, monitoring, and agentic substrate that will let enterprise deploy AI now.

item.title: AWS says its AI security agent fixes 89% of bugs — but there’s a catch
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
AWS made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available on Thursday. The service finds and validates bugs in your repositories, checks

The post AWS says its AI security agent fixes 89% of bugs — but there’s a catch appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AWS made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available on Thursday. The service finds and validates bugs in your repositories, checks them against your AWS environment, and opens pull requests with proposed fixes.

The 89% benchmark claim

The company published its headline benchmark on October 5, more than two weeks before launch. In that run, Continuum passed 819 of 920 tasks on CyberGym-E2E, an 89.0% end-to-end success rate, against a previous public high of 65.9%. Matt Garman, CEO of AWS, writes on X that AI is “genuinely transformative for defenders” and that Continuum scored higher than any other AI agent on the test.

Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist and co-founder of Duckbill, replies to the post, wondering whether the release started as a re:Invent announcement and was pushed out early, given the state of the internet. Quinn offered no evidence that AWS had moved up the announcement.

The recent PHP2Shell case shows how AI is making it easier to find vulnerabilities but fixing them is another story.

The recent PHP2Shell case shows how AI is making it easier to find vulnerabilities but fixing them is another story.

How CyberGym-E2E works

CyberGym-E2E gives an agent 90 minutes to find and fix a vulnerability in one of 139 open-source projects, without a bug description, proof of concept, crash log, or existing patch to work from. The agent must identify the flaw, trigger it, and produce a fix that stops the crash without breaking existing tests. All tasks involve memory-safety bugs in C or C++, leaving out many other languages and vulnerability types, as AWS acknowledges.

Grading runs in four cumulative stages. Continuum found and reproduced a bug in 92.5% of tasks, stopped the crash in 89.6%, and kept the project’s tests passing in 89.0%. The fourth stage checks whether the patch also fixes the historical vulnerability the benchmark selected.

The agent never learns which vulnerability that is; it only has to find and repair a real flaw in the codebase. Continuum’s patch also fixed that historical bug in 37.8% of tasks, against a previous public high of 26.2%.

Continuum’s patch also fixed that historical bug in 37.8% of tasks, against a previous public high of 26.2%.

The historical-bug score gap

The company does have a point about that last stage. A repository can have several vulnerabilities, and fixing a different one doesn’t make the work worthless, which helps explain the gap between the two scores.

Continuum completed 89% of the tasks by finding and patching a real vulnerability without breaking existing tests, but only 37.8% of those patches also addressed the the historical bug the benchmark was checking for. The agent wasn’t told which bug that was, so it’s not quite a fair comparison. What we still don’t know is how well Continuum performs when a team gives it a specific vulnerability to fix.

A repository can have several vulnerabilities, and fixing a different one doesn’t make the work worthless, which helps explain the gap between the two scores.

Who graded the benchmark

AWS ran the tests itself and says Continuum followed the benchmark’s rules, including limits on internet access. The company also checked that the agent wasn’t simply looking up fixes that were already public. Continuum passed 89% of tasks within the 90-minute time limit.

Give it more time, AWS says, and that rises to 93.7%. The benchmark and testing tools are public, but so far, those results are AWS’s alone.
